newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Iran says ready to do deal on S.Africa oil depot.
newsitem.headline: Iran says ready to do deal on S.Africa oil depot.

text.p: Iran's President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani said on Friday his country was ready to do a deal to store Iranian crude oil at Saldanha Bay, north of Cape Town, if South Africa was willing.

"This matter will solely depend on South Africa. Should they find it to be in their interest or the interest of the region, we would be available to sign an agreement to work that out," he told reporters after meeting South Africa's President Nelson Mandela.
Mandela did not comment on the storage project after the two leaders' 20 minutes of talks.

Rafsanjani made no further comment on the storage proposal, but added: "At the present time the pressure on the oil market is quite high and we have sold our oil for very many months to come in advance."

The proposal to store at least 15 million barrels of Iranian oil at the Central Energy Fund's (CEF) 45-million barrel depot at Saldanha Bay has been opposed by conservationists. U.S. officials have also expressed reservations.
The project has been delayed for an environmental impact study, which is not expected to be completed much before the end of the year.
However, the CEF said in its 1995/6 annual report this week that it expected to be storing and trading the crude by March next year.
Commenting on other areas of possible cooperation between South Africa and Iran, Rafsanjani said South Africa had expertise in mining technology which might be of interest to Iran.
Officials said the broad focus of Rafsanjani's whistle-stop state visit on Thursday and Friday was to strengthen bilateral relations and rectify a trade imbalance.

South Africa historically depends on Iran for two-thirds of its crude oil, for which it pays about five billion rand annually, while Iran last year bought South African goods worth only 145.7 million rand.

However, Iran's dominance of the South African oil market has been challenged this year by a strong marketing drive by Kuwait while oil buyers have increasingly been turning to other sources since the lifting of the anti-apartheid oil embargo.
